Block System 2.0 & Block Editor: Self-Serve Visual Customisation

AUG — DEC 2023  ·  Canlab, Korea 
2x
Client acquisition in 3 months
54%
Cut in onboarding time

The problem

As canD's client base diversified, the existing block system couldn't support the visual variety clients needed. Clients were hitting configuration ceilings, limiting their ability to differentiate their services, and limiting canD's ability to win and retain them.

What I did

Led product development of Block System 2.0, a modular visual customisation system, alongside a Block Editor enabling clients to configure pages intuitively without engineering support. New visual-composition blocks (image, video, button, spacer, section, grid) replaced the old data-only blocks, and each component gained granular, atomised design settings.

To ease the transition, I designed an intermediary step "1.0-resembling 2.0" with basic templates and an automatic page-conversion feature, reducing the emotional and resource burden of migrating to the new system.

Outcome

Client acquisition doubled in 3 months, and onboarding time was cut by 54%. Business sales were unblocked as clients gained the flexibility to build advanced, differentiated designs, and the project laid the groundwork for a scalable, service-wide design system extending to navigation and footer areas.

Navigation & DM System and UX Redesign

MAR — JUN 2024  ·  CANLAB, KOREA  
2x

The problem

As canD scaled to support clients running multiple sub-communities, app navigation became a growing source of friction. Client feedback and interviews revealed two critical issues: users couldn't orient themselves across communities, and DMs from sub-communities were being missed, creating churn risk for second-stage contracts.

What I did

Led discovery and product delivery with a team of 1 designer and 3 engineers. Ran interviews with four client companies across beginning, single-community and multi-community stages — asking them to simulate how they'd design their own app navigation if given customisation tools. The interviews confirmed the hypothesis and surfaced an unexpected second issue: missed DMs from sub-communities.

Shipped a navigation overhaul including customisable app navigation per client, a joined sub-communities page, and a unified DM inbox in the service hub.

Outcome

Client acquisition doubled in 3 months, navigation-related support tickets dropped by 85%, and DM usage within sub-communities rose 120%. This project ran in parallel with the Block System 2.0 redesign, together removing the friction that had been blocking both new acquisition and second-stage sales.

The problem

In canD, Web3 community clients needed a way to represent identity, achievement, and membership that was permanent and non-transferable. Standard NFTs could be sold or transferred, undermining their credibility, and the UX was too complex for non-crypto-native community members.

What I did

Led a cross-functional task force to validate the opportunity, define the product, and integrate Web3 APIs into canD's live platform, shipping CryptoBadge — a non-transferable token system built on the Soul-Bound Token standard — with real client deployments across community, ticketing, and membership use cases.

This was one of canD's first Web3 integrations, validating a new domain opportunity and supporting client acquisition through tailored demos and MVPs.

Outcome

Successfully shipped and validated across multiple real clients: Seoulbound (global Web3 event ticketing), Nonce (DAO community membership), Vake (social campaign platform), and Hypersportsclub (NFT holder recognition). Designed and demoed a live service at ETHDenver 2023.

Web3 Commerce

Brickbit: NFT-Backed Crowdfunding for Creator-Owned Products

Canlab, Korea  ·  Blockchain TF

The problem

Creators making MOC (My Own Creation) products sold through licensors had to hand over licensing rights to get their designs manufactured and sold, losing direct control of their own revenue channel. Mass-produced copies also had no way to be reliably told apart from the original.

Buyers, in turn, had little trust in a creator's brand outside the platforms they'd issued through, and little visibility into whether a product would actually be delivered as promised.

Screenshot: Brickbit project purpose and background

What I did

Designed a blockchain crowdfunding model where creators could fund and sell a limited run of a physical product directly, with an NFT minted per unit as proof of ownership and pre-order — giving buyers a verifiable, transferable claim rather than just a licence.

Scoped and designed the full user and admin flow: crowdfunding page, wallet connection and PIN setup via a dedicated CAN Wallet, payment, NFT drop on successful funding, shipping request and tracking, and resale rights for a second-hand market after initial delivery.

Screenshot: user and admin flow
Screenshot: CAN Wallet PIN setup and transaction flow

Outcome

The project didn't reach commercial launch, and there are no usage numbers to point to. What it did prove was that the pattern itself — NFT-backed ownership and crowdfunding for creator-made products — was technically and product-wise buildable end to end. That groundwork fed directly into later Web3 client wins on canD. [If there's a specific reason it didn't launch, or a specific later client it fed into, add it here.]

Process Design Org Change

Redefining QA: From One Owner to Everyone's Responsibility

Canlab, Korea  ·  Core Squad

The problem

I joined as a QA intern and, within about two years, ended up owning QA for the entire product team, testing every development ticket myself. As the team and product grew, this stopped scaling: the backlog of tickets waiting on me kept growing, and testing features I hadn't planned meant constant back-and-forth with the people who had, since I lacked the context they'd built up. Planning documents were rarely kept current either, since fast, verbal decision-making was how the team actually worked.

Original QA R&R proposal document

What I did

I went back to first principles: what is QA, and why do we do it? I redefined it as quality assurance, not testing, meaning the person best placed to own it is whoever understands the feature best, usually its own planner or PM, not a separate, centralised QA role.

I proposed shifting default testing ownership to each feature's own planner, with the QA role stepping in only when asked, and keeping ownership of bugs and maintenance work that weren't tied to a single feature. I presented this first to the planning team, then to the whole product team, and wrote it up as a shared philosophy document that defined what QA meant for the team going forward.

Slack announcement and team philosophy doc

Outcome

I didn't measure the impact quantitatively, but the qualitative shift was clear: less unnecessary back-and-forth during testing, and fewer issues surfacing after QA was marked complete. It also freed me to move into the PM role I'd been building toward. Months later, after I'd fully moved off QA duties, the change still came up unprompted in anonymous 360 feedback from colleagues. The document became the team's standing QA philosophy, used to onboard every new QA hire after me.
